Uncle Sidhu.description: A passionate book lover who owns many books and is reluctant to lend them, except to Feluda.

Baba.description: The narrator's father and childhood friend of Subimal, whom he visits every Sunday.

Subimal.description: Baba's childhood friend whom he visits regularly.

Topshe.description: Feluda's cousin and the narrator of the story, who often accompanies Feluda on his cases.

Sudhir Dhar.description: Sudhir Dhar is a mild-mannered bookshop owner from College Street who seeks Feluda's help regarding his son Mukul's mysterious memories of a past life.

Kailash Chowdhury.description: A customer of Sudhir Dhar who has spoken highly of Feluda.

Dr Hemanga Hajra.description: Dr Hemanga Hajra is a well-known parapsychologist and psychologist researching reincarnation, who accompanies Mukul to Rajasthan and is a key figure in the mystery Feluda investigates.

Shivratan Mukherjee.description: Shivratan Mukherjee is a solicitor and neighbor of Sudhir Dhar, whose grandson Neelu was mistakenly kidnapped during the events of the story.

Neelu.description: Shivratan Mukherjee's grandson, who was kidnapped by mistake.

Charminar.description: A popular Indian brand of cigarettes smoked by Feluda.

Durga Puja.description: A major Hindu festival celebrated in Bengal and other parts of India, honoring the goddess Durga.

Nihar.description: A person whose house is near the narrator's, where a Durga Puja is being held.

Pintu.description: Another person associated with the house where Durga Puja is being held.

Yeh jo muhabbat hai.description: A famous Hindi song from the film Kati Patang.

Kati Patang.description: A 1971 Hindi film known for its popular songs.

Johnny Mera Naam.description: A 1970 Hindi film, referenced for its music.

Hindustan Standard.description: An English-language newspaper published in India.

Shyambazar.description: A locality in Kolkata, India, from where Sudhir Dhar travels.

College Street.description: A famous street in Kolkata known for its many bookstores.

Dhar & Co..description: Sudhir Dhar's bookshop located on College Street.

Mechhobazar.description: A locality in Kolkata where Sudhir Dhar resides.

Jodhpur.description: A city in Rajasthan, India, known for its forts and palaces.

Rajasthan.description: A large state in northwest India, famous for its desert landscape and historic forts.

Rajputana.description: The historical region that largely corresponds to present-day Rajasthan.

Dhalbhoomgarh.description: A place where one of Feluda's cases occurred.

Patna.description: A city in eastern India, where another of Feluda's cases took place.

Gangtok.description: The capital city of Sikkim, mentioned as a previous location of a Feluda case.

Raj Kahini.description: A famous collection of historical tales by Abanindranath Tagore.

Abanindranath Tagore.description: A renowned Bengali writer and artist, author of Raj Kahini.

Toofan Express.description: A long-distance train in India, taken by Dr Hajra and Mukul to Rajasthan.

Chittor.description: Short for Chittorgarh, a historic city in Rajasthan.

Udaipur.description: A city in Rajasthan, known for its lakes and palaces.

Bengal.description: A region in eastern India, home to the narrator and Feluda.

jatismar.description: A jatismar (plural: jatismars) is a person believed to recall events from a previous life, a concept central to the story's theme of reincarnation.

dhoti.description: A traditional men's garment worn in India, consisting of a long piece of cloth wrapped around the waist and legs.

parapsychologist.description: A specialist who studies paranormal psychological phenomena such as telepathy, ESP, and reincarnation.

harmonium.description: A free-reed keyboard instrument, similar to a pump organ, commonly used in Indian music.

Puja.description: A religious festival or ritual worship in Hinduism, often referring to Durga Puja in Bengal.

Manohar.description: Mr Mukherjee's servant, who helps during the visit.

Moti.description: Neelu's classmate, whose house hosts a Durga Puja.

Calcutta.description: The former name of Kolkata, a major city in eastern India.

Jaipur.description: The capital city of Rajasthan, known as the Pink City and famous for its forts and palaces.

Bikaner.description: A city in Rajasthan, also known for its historic fort.

Bundi.description: A town in Rajasthan, notable for its fort and palaces.

Fairlie Place.description: A location in Calcutta, possibly referring to an office or administrative area.

Todd.description: Refers to James Tod, a British officer and historian known for his writings on Rajasthan.

A Guide to India, Pakistan, Burma and Ce.description: A travel guidebook covering the Indian subcontinent and neighboring countries.

India.description: A country in South Asia, the primary setting of the story.

Pakistan.description: A neighboring country to India, mentioned in the context of the guidebook.

Burma.description: The former name of Myanmar, a country bordering India, mentioned in the guidebook.

Ceylon.description: The former name of Sri Lanka, mentioned in the guidebook.

Rajputs.description: The Rajputs, including the Bhati Rajputs, are a prominent warrior group from Rajasthan historically associated with ruling Jaisalmer and other regions, known for their valor.

Marwar.description: A region in Rajasthan, also referring to the Marwar Junction railway station.

Agra.description: A city in northern India, famous for the Taj Mahal and a major railway hub.

kurta pyjama.description: A traditional Indian outfit consisting of a long tunic (kurta) and loose-fitting trousers (pyjama).

Babu.description: A respectful term of address in India, often used for gentlemen or educated men.

Lalmohan Ganguli.description: A Bengali thriller writer and Feluda's friend who often provides comic relief and accompanies him on adventures.

Agra Fort.description: A historic fort in Agra, India, and a major railway station in the city.

Taj Mahal.description: A world-famous white marble mausoleum in Agra, India, built by Mughal emperor Shah Jahan.

Sardar Shankar Road.description: A street in Calcutta mentioned as the location of Uncle Sidhu's house.

Tara Road.description: A road in Calcutta near Sardar Shankar Road, where the narrator's family lives.

Argentina.description: A country in South America, mentioned as the home of Juan Vucatich.

England.description: A country in the United Kingdom, referenced in the context of fingerprint classification.

Chicago.description: A major city in the United States, where Bhavananda set up his fraudulent center.

Delhi.description: The capital city of India, mentioned as a stop in Jatayu's travels.

Fatehpur Sikri.description: A historic city near Agra, known for its Mughal architecture.

Bhadreshwar.description: A town in West Bengal, India, where Jatayu lives.

Himalayas.description: A major mountain range in Asia, referenced as the only 'muscles' of Bengal.

Ravan.description: A demon king from the Indian epic Ramayana, fought by the mythical bird Jatayu.

Urdu.description: A language widely spoken in South Asia, mentioned in reference to a newspaper.

Bedouins.description: Nomadic Arab tribes, referenced in Jatayu's novels.

Arabia.description: A region in Western Asia, referenced in Jatayu's novel title 'Bloodbath in Arabia'.

Prakhar Rudra.description: The fictional hero of Jatayu's thriller novels.

Charles Atlas.description: A famous bodybuilder whose advertisements inspired Jatayu.

yoghurt.description: A fermented dairy product, commonly eaten in India.

divan.description: A long, low sofa without a back or arms, used for seating or sleeping.

Namaskar.description: A respectful Indian greeting, similar to 'hello' or 'greetings'.

gulabi rewri.description: A sweet, crunchy Indian confection made from sesame seeds and sugar, often flavored with rose (gulabi).

Mukul Dhar.description: Mukul Dhar is Sudhir Dhar's eight-year-old son, believed to be a jatismar who recalls a previous life in a Rajasthani fort and becomes central to the case Feluda investigates.

Mandar Bose.description: A globetrotter and hunter recently returned to India after many years abroad, noted for his suspicious behavior and tall tales.

Bharatpur.description: A city in Rajasthan, India, known for its bird sanctuary and historical significance.

Rajasthanis.description: Rajasthanis are people native to the state of Rajasthan in northwestern India, known for their distinctive dress, customs, and language (Rajasthani).

Aravalli Hills.description: A mountain range in western India, running across Rajasthan and known for its rugged terrain.

Kisangarh.description: A city in Rajasthan, India, famous for its marble industry and historical forts.

Circuit House.description: A government guest house, often used for lodging by officials and travelers in India.

New Bombay Lodge.description: A lodging establishment in Jodhpur where Lalmohan Babu chooses to stay.

Mughals.description: The Mughals, also referred to as the Mughal dynasty, ruled large parts of India from the 16th to 19th centuries and are noted for their cultural and architectural legacy.

Visitors’ Book.description: A register in hotels or guest houses where guests sign their names and details.

Kenya.description: A country in East Africa, referenced as a place where Mandar Bose lived and worked.

Albania.description: A country in southeastern Europe, mentioned by Mandar Bose as a place where he had good tea.

Darjeeling.description: A region in West Bengal, India, famous worldwide for its high-quality tea.

naagras.description: Traditional Rajasthani footwear, typically made of leather and often ornately decorated.

roti.description: A round, unleavened flatbread commonly eaten in India.

tonga.description: A horse-drawn carriage used for transport in many parts of India.

Swami Bhavananda.description: A Bengali man who started a fraudulent spiritual healing center in Chicago and was later exposed by Dr. Hajra.

Barmer.description: A town in Rajasthan, another location visited during the investigation.

Marwari.description: A term referring to people from the Marwar region of Rajasthan, often associated with business.

chappal.description: A type of open-toed Indian sandal, commonly worn indoors.

Mr Mitter.description: A sharp and analytical private investigator who is the protagonist of the stories and solves the cases.

Mr Maheshwari.description: A character who accompanies Mandar Bose and the others to Bikaner, involved in the day's events.

Kathmandu.description: The capital city of Nepal, referenced as the origin of Jatayu's Nepali dagger.

Devikund.description: A site near Bikaner known for its cenotaphs (chhatris) built in memory of Rajput warriors.

Raja Rai Singh.description: A historical Rajput ruler who began building the Bikaner fort, also served in Akbar's army.

Akbar.description: A famous Mughal emperor who ruled much of India in the 16th century.

Alam Ambali.description: The name of a beautiful silver throne in the Bikaner fort, said to be a gift from a Mughal badshah.

Phool Mahal.description: A palace or hall within the Bikaner fort, known for its ornate architecture.

Gaj Mandir.description: Another notable hall or palace within the Bikaner fort.

Sheesh Mahal.description: A 'mirror palace' or hall, often found in Rajasthani forts, decorated with intricate mirror work.

Ganga Nivas.description: A section or hall within the Bikaner fort.

Chini Burj.description: A tower or structure within the Bikaner fort, possibly decorated with Chinese-style tiles.

Bagri.description: The name of the person at the reception desk in the Circuit House who hands Feluda a letter.

catapult.description: A handheld slingshot used to launch small projectiles, often used by children in India.

Nepali dagger.description: A traditional curved knife from Nepal, also known as a khukuri, used as a weapon or tool.

gypsies.description: A term commonly used in India to refer to nomadic communities, often with distinct cultural practices.

cenotaphs.description: Monumental tombs or memorials built in honor of someone whose remains are elsewhere; in Rajasthan, often called 'chhatris'.

chhatris.description: Elevated, dome-shaped pavilions used as memorials for Rajput warriors, commonly seen in Rajasthan.

badshah.description: A Persian-derived word meaning 'emperor' or 'king', often used for Mughal rulers.

paan.description: A preparation combining betel leaf with areca nut and sometimes tobacco, chewed for its stimulant effects and cultural significance.

bearer.description: A hotel attendant or servant, commonly used in South Asian English to refer to someone who serves food or assists guests.

Tanganyika.description: A historical region in East Africa, now part of Tanzania.

Martin Johnson.description: An American adventurer and author known for his travel books about Africa.

Dussehra.description: A significant Hindu festival celebrated across India, marking the victory of good over evil.

Solanki Stores.description: A shop in the story selling stoneware, presumably named after the Solanki dynasty or family.

Jaisalmer.description: A city in Rajasthan, India, famous for its yellow sandstone architecture and desert fort.

Pokhran.description: A town in Rajasthan, India, known for its proximity to the Thar Desert and historical significance.

Rewari Passenger.description: A passenger train running between Jodhpur and Rewari, a city in Haryana, India.

Thar desert.description: A vast arid region in northwestern India, also known as the Great Indian Desert.

yoga.description: A traditional Indian practice involving physical postures, breathing exercises, and meditation.

bazaar.description: A marketplace or shopping area, commonly found in South Asian cities.

saab.description: A respectful term for 'sir' or 'master' in Hindi and other Indian languages.

Gurbachan Singh.description: The Punjabi Sikh driver responsible for driving Feluda and his companions through the desert roads of Rajasthan.

Sikh.description: A follower of Sikhism, a monotheistic religion that originated in the Punjab region of India.

Alauddin Khilji.description: A Sultan of Delhi in the early 14th century, known for his military campaigns, including an attack on Jaisalmer.

Ramdeora.description: A small town and railway station in Rajasthan, located near Pokhran.

Japan Airlines.description: An international airline from Japan, referenced as the brand of Lalmohan Babu's bag.

Bradshaw.description: A well-known railway timetable guide used in India.

Martin & Co..description: A historical reference to a company that once operated small trains in India.

paunch.description: A large or protruding belly, often used to describe someone's stomach.

Sardarji.description: A respectful term for a Sikh man, often used to address Sikh drivers or elders.

cowrie.description: A type of small, glossy shell often used for decoration or as currency in traditional Indian culture.

holdall.description: A holdall (plural: holdalls) is a large bag or case used for carrying personal belongings, especially while traveling.

goja.description: A Bengali deep-fried pastry dipped in syrup, often eaten as a sweet snack.

flask.description: A container used to carry liquids, commonly water, while traveling.

turban.description: A traditional headwear made of cloth wound around the head, commonly worn in Rajasthan and other parts of India.

shawl.description: A piece of fabric worn over the shoulders or head, often used for warmth or as a disguise.

shuttlecock.description: A conical object used in the game of badminton, here used metaphorically to describe being tossed about.

moustaches.description: Facial hair grown on the upper lip, often styled elaborately in Rajasthan.

camel.description: A large domesticated animal used for riding and transport, especially in desert regions like Rajasthan.

Jetha-chandan.description: A small railway station in Rajasthan, India, where the train stops.

Thaiyat Hamira.description: Another railway station in Rajasthan, India, on the route to Jaisalmer.

durrie.description: A traditional Indian cotton rug or floor covering.

Inspector Rathor.description: A police inspector introduced by Dr Hajra, involved in the resolution of the case.

Ambassador.description: A classic Indian car model, commonly used as taxis and government vehicles.

dak bungalow.description: A dak bungalow (plural: dak bungalows) is a colonial-era rest house for travelers, originally built for government officials and now used by travelers across India.

Raja.description: A traditional Indian title for a king or princely ruler.

Mohangarh.description: A place near Jaisalmer, known for its fort and desert landscape.

ekka.description: A one-horse carriage used for local travel in India.

cycle-rickshaw.description: A three-wheeled vehicle powered by a person pedaling, used for public transport.

chowkidar.description: A watchman or caretaker, especially of a building or compound.

Professor Trivedi.description: An acquaintance of Dr Hajra in Jodhpur who assists him during his travels.

Raghunath Sarai.description: A lodging place in Jodhpur where Dr Hajra stayed.

Japan.description: A country in East Asia, referenced as the origin of the fake revolver.

veranda.description: A roofed, open-air porch attached to a house, common in Indian architecture.
